blocks.value: **Square brackets allow for character variability.** To return `true` for `"dog"` or `"Dog"` but not `"dOg"`, `equalsIgnoreCase` would not work and `equals` would take multiple lines:
return animal.matches("[Cc]at|[Dd]og");
Brackets are not restricted to two-character options. **Combined with a hyphen, they include any range of characters.**
Consider a rhyming game that returns `true` if a word begins with any lowercase letter and ends in `"at"`. A first attempt might be:
The regex is shorter and more general:
return word.matches("[a-z]at");
To include uppercase characters:
return word.matches("[a-zA-Z](at|AT)");
**Using the range `a-Z` or `A-z` will not work correctly**: those ranges span the punctuation characters that sit between the alphabets in Unicode.
Everything inside the square brackets defines exactly how **one** character can be represented:
return word.matches("[ 0-9a-zA-Z]bcde");
This allows the first character to be a space, any digit, or any letter. The rest must be `"bcde"`, case-sensitively.
The wildcard
**The dot (`.`) is the wildcard operator representing any single character.** To check whether a String `element` is a number followed by any other single character:
return element.matches("[0-9].");
Writing every class out longhand works, but Java provides shorthands you will meet constantly:
`^` just inside the brackets **negates** the class: `[^0-9]` means "any character that is not a digit."
**In Java, you must write these with two backslashes.** `\` starts an escape sequence in a string literal, so the regex `\d` is written `"\\d"`:

return str.matches("\\d{4}");        // exactly four digits
return str.matches("[0-9]{4}");      // identical, written longhand
Forgetting the second backslash is the most common Java-specific regex error there is.
Matching a real dot

A bare `.` matches any character, so to match an actual full stop you must escape it with a backslash, written `"\\."` in Java. The difference shows up as soon as the text contains something other than a dot:

System.out.println("3.5".matches("\\d\\.\\d"));   // true
System.out.println("3x5".matches("\\d\\.\\d"));   // false, x is not a dot
System.out.println("3x5".matches("\\d.\\d"));     // true, the wildcard accepts x
